utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Jim Cowles, with me will be Mr. George Huber, as the case manager. We represent the Prosecution today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, my name is Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning Your Honours, I am Zeljko Olujic, attorney from Croatia, appearing on behalf of Zdravko Mucic together with my co-counsel, Mr. Duric attorney from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic appearing on behalf of Hazim Delic along with Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I represent Esad Landzo along with my co-counsel Ms. Nancy Boler. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Asif Jusufovic

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly take your seat, please. Yes. You may proceed, Ms. Boler.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jusufovic, would you please state your name for the Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Asif Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: My name is Nancy Boler and along with Cynthia McMurrey I represent Esad Landzo. You and I have met before, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: We visited in Konjic when I was there in May and then again briefly two or three weeks ago and then again after you arrived at the Bel Air Hotel; isn't that right, here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: When we spoke yesterday morning, your leg was hurting. Is it any better today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No better, I am afraid. I couldn't get a doctor to see to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I understand they've arranged for you to go to the doctor this afternoon. Is that still going to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have been told so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, you've never testified before, have you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I understand you're a little bit nervous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, my usual self.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Jusufovic, let me direct your attention back to the Konjic area in the spring of 1992. When the war began, were you a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: What were your duties as a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was one of the organisers of the resistance in Konjic and the formation of the first command in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Now, what did that entail, what types of things did you do in that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to organise the friends and people of Konjic --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, if you're having a problem with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would you kindly adjust the headphone for him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: All right. I think you were telling me about what types of things you did in your capacity in the TO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We organised ourselves. That is, into smaller groups of people and we got armed and prepared for the resistance because it was clear that there would be an aggression between Bosnia Herzegovina and particularly against Konjic where I lived. As I already said, we armed ourselves, we prepared for a struggle to be ready when the attack of the enemy came.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And at some point did you become a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When we reached the Village of Glavaticevo, that was the first time that we were on the frontlines towards the enemy. We established the lines with the -- manning them with local inhabitants and upon return to Konjic some ten days later, we organised the military police. And I transferred to the military police immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And how were your duties as a member of the military police different from your duties as a member of the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was in the TO at the Glavaticevo, some disorders started in Konjic. There were various attempts to steal property, so that it was necessary to protect the town and the population and private property.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: At some point did Esad Landzo become a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did, but later.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Was the time at which Esad Landzo became a member of the military police, was that after the murders of the military policeman at Repovci?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours, to the leading form of the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: She has to find out the times.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Direct him to as to what was the relevant time when he did that. You can do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I can do that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you recall the month when Esad Landzo joined the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, very well. It was the beginning of August, between the 1st and the 5th or two or three weeks after the killing in Repovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And at some point, was there a swearing in ceremony for the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you recall the time of that ceremony, the date of that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do because the military police was moved from the premises of Borovo and Oslobodenje, that is in the centre of town, to the Third of March Elementary School where we put up and that is where we were sworn in, in the gym of that school. The date could have been the 20th, 24th, 25th, I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Of what month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the month of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: So you attended that ceremony, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And did Esad Landzo also attend that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of us belonging to the military police were there, including him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And did Nermin Mandic also attend that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, he was one of the police chiefs, one of the leaders.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Can you tell me approximately how many members of the military police were sworn in at that ceremony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 30, 35, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, at this time, I would like to ask the assistance of the usher and I would like to show a short video clip. I have given the Prosecution a copy and I have given the booth a copy. The amount of time that's shown on this videotape is approximately seven minutes, but I won't be showing all of that. I will just be showing a few portions of the swearing in ceremony, the portions that show Mr. Jusufovic, so that he can verify that he was at the ceremony, as was Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is Esad Landzo in this tape?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can you see Esad Landzo on this tape?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I believe not. But you can see Asif Jusufovic, and he can testify that that, indeed, was the ceremony and that Esad Landzo was there. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution challenging his being military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You're challenging that he is?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: They're not working. Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution will object unless and until this witness has properly identified it. We fail to see the relevance if the defendant is not depicted in the tape. I think it will go to the weight, but we'll defer it for the Court, if proper foundation is laid for the admissibility of the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You might show it. You can then tell us those who were sworn too at the same time with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: If the video booth, then, will start this tape. It begins at two minutes and six seconds, rather than zero, simply because when I viewed it the first time and I wrote down the times bring to the Court's attention, it was based on two minutes and six seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a text.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I heard that the interpreters do not have a text. It's not going to be necessary for any interpretation. It's just a picture of everybody in the military police uniform with a white belt, which is the -- one of the things that they wore. And they are simply going to pick up their oath at a little table. And you'll see Esad's picture there and some of the others and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, let's go to the tape and see what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: For the information of the video booth -- it began at 206 or 7 and at approximately 2.45, I believe it will have our first picture of Mr. Asif Jusufovic. He is in the front row. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: If the video could freeze at this point, that's the picture of Mr. Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, were you able to watch that tape on your screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: That was my fault, I should have reminded you. Now, are you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see well now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Is that you, Mr. Jusufovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the cap. The one in the middle wearing a cap.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And what is this -- what does this video depict? What's going on here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a line up and a swearing in, in the gym of the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And those are the military police being sworn in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I am going to role just a little bit more of the tape, so that you can see some of the swearing in activity. If the video booth will continue just a little bit with that tape. Would the video freeze -- could you back up just a little bit to freeze on the man with the beard. About the third in, if you could back up maybe about 5 or 10 seconds so that we're still viewing the people on the front row. Sorry, if the video booth could just back up 5 or 10 seconds so that we're still viewing the men on the front row. Okay. If you'll just freeze right there, please. Mr. Jusufovic, do you recognise the tall gentleman standing here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: What is the name of the man who's last there, closest to your left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nermin Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: If I can ask the video to role a little farther to where the people are walking up to the desk where they're receiving their certificates. I believe it's at -- 3.15. All right. At some point, just a little farther along, you see the men going up to the front table to pick up their certificate. Could the video show that. If the video room could just fast forward a little bit to where the members of the military police are walking to the front to pick up their -- to sign their certificate. You can see them walking away with a white piece of paper in their hands. If you could freeze -- all right, stop just there. Mr. Jusufovic, what is going on now in that video? Did you receive a certificate that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to sign the oath. Yes, and then we received the certificate.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Is that a picture of Nermin Mandic walking away -- Nermin Mandic is walking away with his certificate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to move that this be admitted into evidence. He has identified it as the swearing in ceremony of the military police where he was present?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do you really want this in evidence? Landzo is not in it. So many faces have been shown. He is not amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I did look at that again and again, and I believe there is enough faces that are not shown that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I know. If his face had been there, that would have been really evidence. He is not there, why --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Since Landzo is a lot shorter than everybody else and that there were a lot of people that were not shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I know, I know. It's up to you, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to have it into evidence. Is it admitted, Your Honour? Is it admitted, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It wasn't admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: It was not admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Okay, I'll move on. May I ask the registrar, please what the number of that exhibit was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You're trying to show there was a ceremony in which this witness was a participant and which he swore as a military policeman, this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: As to what?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'll also ask him another question about that and put something else into evidence in just a few minutes if I could just ask a few more questions before I get to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If your client was the person identified, it could have been a very relevant thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, I would like to give the --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document was marked D 69/4. The videotape was marked D 68/4.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: All right, I would like you to take a look at this document, please, Mr. Jusufovic, and tell me if you can recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have one like it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And what is it, please? What is it, Mr. Jusufovic? What is that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is from the official swearing in ceremony. I received one like it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the date is on the certificate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 26th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Can you tell me whose name is on the certificate, who it was issued to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo father's name, Sulijo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Does this represent to you that he came a member of the military place on August 26th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, judging by this document, he came at the beginning of August and it was normal for him to take the oath like the rest of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to introduce this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How can you do it? It's not been signed by him. It's not been issued by him. How can he prove it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: He stated he recognises it because he got one just like it on the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If that is all, then how can he prove this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: He testified that Esad Landzo also attended the ceremony on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's good enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He could have picked up this paper anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I don't say that it's not genuine, but he can't prove it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: All right. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, I am going to direct your attention back to the time when you and Esad Landzo were together in the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a question. When you were in the military police, together with Esad Landzo, were you aware of any health problems or breathing problems that Mr. Landzo had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I noticed that at the first position where we held -- which we held at the cross-roads. As he was mostly alone, he was a loner, he would separate from the rest of us and we would notice his coughing. I had no idea that he had this disease. And then talking with friends, we would discuss it. And later on, we learned that he had this disease -- I am not very familiar with medicine, so I don't know whether it's asthma or something else, but we noticed that he had a shortness of breath. And especially when we went on assignment and if we had to go up hill, it became quite evident that he was short of breath and it became quite manifest.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Do you recall going to the Village of Buturovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I went there twice and he went there when I went to second time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Can you describe that journey for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were going in lorries along a roundabout way to the Village of Dubocani and then from there we went on foot. And while the terrain was flat, he moved like the others. But as soon as there was a slope to climb, he would lag behind the rest of us. As there were plenty of horses around, so we loaded the food and other equipment on them and then we discussed the possibility of sending him back, but he refused. He was given orders to go back, but he wouldn't obey. And then, we put him on a horse and that is how he covered the rest of the journey, on horseback.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Well, when he was on the horse, he was able to continue with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He didn't use his own legs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: All right. Now let's go back to the headquarters for the military police. For the most part, what type of tasks was Esad assigned to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first he was given the same assignments as the rest of us, but later on when we learned of his disease, we realised that he couldn't be assigned to tasks that were urgent. And which required a lot of walking, especially up hill, because he couldn't move as quickly as the others. He would lag behind. Then, he would breathe heavily so that in the end, we wouldn't give him such task, but rather he was assigned to security of commands. He was mostly on duty in the unit. He would be given the less strenuous assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Can you describe what kind of person did you know him to be when he was with you in the military police?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you leading evidence regarding his good character.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Am I asking evidence regarding what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Are you asking him about his good character and not his bad character?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: His good character, I understand Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Approximately how old was Esad when he was with you in the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I know he joined us still as a child. He was 17, 18, maybe younger, but I don't know. I just know that he was childish. He was a child in the real sense of the word by his behaviour and generally. As for his work and tasks, the daily tasks, what he was told to do and ordered to do, he did it conscientiously.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me ask you now some questions an about Repovci. This may be difficult for you because your brother was one of the military policeman killed there; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: What was your brother's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aziz Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Isn't it true that Nermin Mandic's brother, the person that we saw in the tape there, was also killed at Repovci, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I pose an objection as to the relevancy of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: As to the relevancy, I think you will find in my very next question. If I might be allowed to ask one more question, I think the relevancy will be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: What was the relationship between Nermin Mandic's brother -- let me ask you first, what was his first name, the one who was killed, his first name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ibrahim Mandic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Was he nicknamed Ibro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ibro, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the relationship was between Esad Landzo and Ibro?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, they're neighbours, they lived in the same house. So, they new each other very well. But he listened more to Ibro than to his brother and to his father. So you can see what their relationship was from that. Whatever was needed, whatever he needed, he turned to him. He protected him, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Would you say Ibro was like a father figure to Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, something like that. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They were the same age. How could they have been?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, there is a great age difference between them. Ibrahim was born in 1955 and the younger one is 24 now. So there is an age difference between them. He brought him up. They were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: So if -- do you recall that Esad Landzo's mother baby-sat for Ibro's child?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Objection to the leading form of the questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this is not harmful at all. Let her ask it. It doesn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's normal in my country, that always happens in all neighbourhoods, in all families, people who have more children. This was a poor family and probably when they went to work, they left their children to the Mandic's, to the mother.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you to tell me how you first heard about what had happened at Repovci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was on duty that night. At 3.00 a.m. I went home to have a rest. And then they contacted me at 10 -- at noon or at 1.00 p.m. to come to the station urgently because something had happened to the control on the way to Repovci, to the patrol. They were not quite sure, quite certain, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And at that point, did you, did you go to Repovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there and Mandic came too and we drove to Brjdani. At the cross-roads to Repovci, there were lots of people there and military. We were not let through to see what had happened on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: But did you see other people milling about? Were you able to see the reactions of the people there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I did. The military were there. The brother of the killed was there too. They gathered the civilians in a small area. There were many units that started going there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with a newspaper called Bosnian Weekly? Are you familiar with that? Free Herzegovina newspaper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not the name of the newspaper. Free Herzegovina is the name. Yeah, it's the only one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would like to, with the assistance of the usher's, show Mr. Jusufovic some pictures that were published in this newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How are is that relevant to us? We're not inquiring into that, the night the policemen were killed. We're more concerned with Celebici. This person said that a person, one of the policeman that was killed there, he was very close to Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, why did you invite this witness? If you have your ideas, lead your evidence to establish why you called him. That is the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You wanted to show that Landzo was very upset over the death of one of the policeman. That's what he said. Why bring in the paper?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The paper shows the brutality Mr. Landzo saw when he went to the scene that day. And explains his state of mind when he returned to Celebici on July 12th, where he is alleged to have hit Mr. Bosko Semukovic (Phon).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: So that justifies some of the allegations made against him? You're putting provocation?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Provocation probably goes to the diminished mental responsibility at the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Call the person who has given the provocation, not the innocent person. Provocation against the person who has given the provocation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, they were all told to go into the wounds to search for Chetniks and this man can testify about their reaction in the community --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let him talk about the reaction, instead of getting these pictures on. I am sure it must have caused a lot of sorrow and grief for the death for some many people doing their national duty. I'm sure of that. That testifies -- some of the allegations made against your client. What sort of diminished responsibility would that be? I can understand if someone does some harm to you, you get provoked then I can understand diminished liability. But how would that justify action or taking revenge on innocent persons?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but we're not talking about a normal person. We're talking about a person with a personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: We will decide later whether he is normal or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: These photographs -- we only wanted to show the Trial Chamber these photographs to show the absolute brutality of the scene, to show how shocking that was for a young 18-year-old to come upon this and see his father figure brutally murdered like this. And if the Court would allow, I think these will give you a different impression of what exactly happened on July 12th. And that's the reason and the motivation for needing to, and desiring to present these to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did you listen to the date this witness was sworn in?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The date he was sworn in as policeman? Did you hear him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, but that's another question. Ms. Boler has not asked the follow-up question to that yet, which will make it clear. First of all, Mr. Landzo was at the scene here on July 12th as a member of the guard from Celebici. They called up everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is not what we're talking about. We're talking ability his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am talking about a different side of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And you're not the one giving evidence, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am just trying to tie it in as to relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's not --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just thought I was answering the Court's question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, did you read the newspaper accounts of your brother's killing and the killing of the eight other military policemen that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- this is the only newspaper that dared to write about it in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I went to the editor's office and asked them to write something. They were the only ones who reported on it, on the case in Repovci. I read it and followed everything. I know everything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Did they also publish graphic pictures of the dead bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I gave them some pictures too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did he see the dead body of his brother? Was it mutilated? Ask him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the scene or later? On the spot or later?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: At any time were you allowed to view--

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I still have the photographs. I brought them with me and, if necessary, I'll show them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: What kind of wounds did your brother receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only his face wasn't mutilated, the rest, all the rest from the shots, from everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, have you gotten any help from the authorities in solving these murders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Are you still --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did try. We did try. Over the past six years now, we tried to, inspectors came from Sarajevo, from Mostar and everybody came. They investigated to the end, that's what they said. The case has been solved. But the killers are walking around Konjic. I went there. I brought the documents to the presidency and to the office, security office to the police, the republican police. We went to all the places. We even sent to documents to the tribunal, but nobody has sent -- given us an answer in the past six years, nobody. It seems to me that this is a greater crime than Celebici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He made a statement that the killers are still walking in Konjic. Ask him about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what our authorities are saying. The mayor and the head of the police, they told us that the killers are known. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And what was the reaction of the public to what you've been going through?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the relevancy of this whole line of questioning. There has been no mention of the defendant yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The defendant is resident of Konjic. Would he not be swayed by the general mood? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that the public was outraged by these murders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, especially Konjic and the surrounding areas. The whole country was outraged.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just have one minute?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, let me back you up to the swearing in ceremony that we discussed earlier. You stated that the ceremony was in late August, August 26th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's the date he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't even know until I saw the date that was in 1992. I can't -- it was August, the middle of August. I know it from Repovci, I followed it. And we were transferred -- I know it was in August, but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Is it a fact that members of the military police joined in the weeks before, in June and July? Was it a gradual assembling of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. People were selected who would be admitted to the military police and they were admitted gradually. Those who were considered fit for the service, were admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And then at the swearing in ceremony, would people who joined in June, July, whatever, at various times, they were all sworn in together on the 26th of August, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. We were all sworn in together, all of us who were there. Mandic could tell you better because he was one of the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: All right. Pass the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you finished with him? Any cross-examinations?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Delalic's Defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: We have a short question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: May it please the Court? Good morning, sir, I am Zeljko Olujic. I am the Defence counsel for Zdravko Mucic. I would like to talk to you and put a few questions. Of course, you are able, are you all right now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know Professor Duro Golubovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Professor?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Duro Golubovic, Professor Duro Golubovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should know him. I can't remember his face now. Golubovic, physical education, P.E., I think I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Professor Duro Golubovic, that's his name, a teacher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are many Duro Golubovic. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a Duro Golubovic whose family were victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Konjic, Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did his family suffer? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not hearsay. I know where they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Where were they killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the road, Zaic Mirlospira (Phon).

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know how they were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You don't know who killed them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hearsay, the same as in Repovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Miralem Macic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's something more about him?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not a member of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: He was never a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was a member of some other unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURIC
utterances.text: Just, a minute we have this problem with the spelling of the transcript. This name has not been put down in the correct form as it was spelled out Mr. Macic, Miralem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you for drawing attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you don't know whether he was a member of the military police. You are excluding this possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was never a member of the military police where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Hazim Delic's Defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any questions for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, may it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: My name is Jim Cowles and I represent the Prosecution in this matter. Mr. Jusufovic, you testified that you believed that Mr. Landzo became a member of the military police at the beginning of August, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, between the 1st and the 5th, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Do you recall giving a statement or talking to a Defence lawyer for Mr. Landzo in August of 1996? An attorney, Mr. Brackovic if, if I pronounce it correctly, an attorney from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Brackovic, something like that. Yes, I did talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Do you remember, at that time, stating that you cannot recall when it was that Mr. Landzo joined the military police, that it was sometime in the warm months, but you were not sure of the exact dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I said then because I didn't know the dates. And then I consulted with the commanders and my point of reference was the event in Repovci, so it happened two or three weeks after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Now, isn't it true that you never went inside the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me be quite clear. I reached as far as the gates on two occasions, that was my duty, to go as far as the gates and that's as far as I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: And that's when you were participating in the turning over of prisoners to the camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: You were not, in other words, you were not inside or did not go inside the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: This is what he said. He went only up to the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: So you don't know what happened inside Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our duty was to take them as far as the gate. That was the duty of the military police. We had no responsibilities inside, no rights, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Now, you were aware that Mr. Landzo was a guard at Celebici camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew where he was at the beginning of the war. Which formation he joined later on, I didn't know until I learned it from his brother who was with me in the military police, and then he too joined later.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: You knew Mr. Landzo had served as a guard at Celebici camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's asked and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: It was wasn't answered, I don't believe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: You didn't know that Mr. Landzo has served as a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know. He worked for a private entrepreneur in Konjic, that is where he worked, and I don't know when he went to Celebici. He was working in a small restaurant, a cafe, or whatever you like to call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Well, do you remember telling his lawyer in August of 1996 that Mr. Landzo transferred from the Celebici barracks to the military police to join you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that his brother brought him to the military police to join us from the Celebici camp. And then the brother had told us about him before that, that he wanted to transfer him.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicated that Mr. Landzo had breathing problems; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: But you don't know how any breathing problems may have affected him in his work at Celebici, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I try to explain to you that heavy labour and walking up hill was difficult for him. He could work if he went on a low ground, but as soon as he had to walk up hill, it became difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: My question is, you don't know how it may have affected him in Celebici camp, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not up to me to think about those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Well now, you are aware that Mr. Landzo drank a lot from an early age and he was using pills; wasn't he in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of the pills. And at the beginning of the war most people spent time in basements, and he was with friends who did drink alcohol. And when he took these pills when he was with us, he said that he was taking these pills, but he didn't tell us that it was for some disease. He avoided talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Are you aware, Mr. Jusufovic, that Mr. Landzo served with the Bosnian army in several actions in warfare? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. Which army? The BiH army or before?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Yes, the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, he went with me for the first time to Glavaticevo. And before then, I only know him from the cafe, from the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Are you aware that he served as a soldier in other actions, besides Glavaticevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came from the camp to join us in the military police. Where he was before that and after that, I don't know. I just know about the time when he was in the military police. I can testify to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: So is the only action or military action that you know Mr. Landzo to have participated in, is the action concerning Glavaticevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honours, that's all I have. I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like to ask the usher's assistance to show Mr. Jusufovic, the Bosnian copy of the statement that he gave to Brackovic, that Mr. Cowles just used in his line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has not asked him because he could impeach him with reference to that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I don't think he did impeached him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He hasn't, but he could if you now begin with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You're not producing the statement to corroborate -- that you can't give. The witness is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: We're introducing it to show that the Prosecutor did not impeach him and I am going to ask him if he still stands by this statement that he gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has not asked him about it at all. Why do you want to produce it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just think it would be useful for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: For the purposes of corroboration for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you want the Prosecution to comment it on later? You want them to do that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: We're not introducing it as substantive evidence, just that the Prosecution was not able to impeach Mr. Jusufovic with this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The Prosecution has not asked that that statement be before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: My understanding is that if the Prosecution attempts to impeach with this statement, then I am allowed to introduce a prior statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If he wanted to impeach it, he would have said, "Please take this into evidence. This is what he said earlier." He has not done that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I understand that, but he did use this statement to question Mr. Jusufovic and attempt to impeach him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you want to, show it to him. When it comes into evidence, he will be entitled at any time to rely on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would just point out to the Court that it is 11.30 and ask, Your Honours, if this would be a convenient time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Don't you think we've already had a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I don't feel like I've had a break, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to offer an objection. This is an improper attempt to try to corroborate her own witness and I would object to the introduction of the statement, itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You will continue your re-examination when we resume, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document has been marked defence document D 70/4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can start your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, I just have one final question. Do you see Esad Landzo in the courtroom today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And does he look different today than when you knew him in the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a great difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Just describe his appearance and behaviour in the military police as opposed to what you see today. That's my final question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he came to the military police, I don't know whether anyone exchanged two sentences with him. He was always somewhere in the corner. I don't know, he looked lost --

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to this question. It's improper re-direct. And she asked appearance and not personality or character.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Does he appear to be a different person today than from what you knew back then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only that he seems -- I see that he is different. It looks like heaven and earth. He is very different. He looks much better. At that time he looked lost. He looked like a lost child then. We were 15 of us there, but nobody was on intimate terms with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jusufovic. Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Asif, and we're very grateful for your assistance. Thank you. Can we have your next witness, please. (Witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence has two subpoenaed witnesses present in The Hague right now. But we had discussions with them last night and I would really like it if the Court would let us have an ex parte hearing before the Court on some of the matters regarding our witnesses that are not able to testify at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: An ex parte hearing, you mean the Prosecution should not be involved in it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I don't think they have anything to do with the problems that I am having with my witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And the witnesses who are expected to testify before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And the Prosecution has nothing to do with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I don't see how they do. It's my problem with the witnesses. It has nothing to do with the Prosecution's opinion one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are they before the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like for them to testify before the Tribunal. But I don't intend to discuss ex parte with the Court any testimony of the witness, only the problems that are arising trying to get testimony out of witnesses. It's a problem that the defence is experiencing. I think that it's something that needs to be brought to the attention of the Court and you can offer guidance to us. If the Prosecutor wants to be present, I don't have a problem with it. But I think it's a matter that needs to be discussed between the Defence of Esad Landzo and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
